title: Password and hash cracking basics
quick: Systems store a hash of a password, not the password itself. Recovery means guessing candidates and comparing their hashes. Long, unique passwords and good storage make this slow or impractical.

sections.title: Hashes and salts
text: A hash function turns any input into a fixed-size value and cannot be reversed directly. A system keeps the hash of your password. At login it hashes what you type and compares the two. A salt is a random value stored with the hash and added before hashing. NIST describes a salt as a value that stops an attacker reusing results between instances.
Because of the salt, two users with the same password get different hashes.

sections.title: What recovery means in practice
text: In forensics, recovery is used in a lawful setting, for example to open an encrypted file that an authorised case requires. Recovery is guessing, not reversing. The process hashes many candidate passwords and compares them with the target hash. Candidates come from wordlists, which are lists of common or leaked passwords, and from rules that change words in common ways.
This page explains concepts only. Practise only on files and hashes you created yourself or are allowed to test.

sections.title: Why strong passwords resist it
text: Every extra character multiplies the number of possibilities. Random long passwords do not appear in wordlists. Slow, memory-hard hashing methods make each guess expensive. NIST guidance also asks services to salt and hash stored passwords with a suitable method, block common and breached passwords and limit failed attempts.
Procedures and laws differ by country and agency, follow your lab's own procedure and authority for any recovery work.

compare.title: Plain, hashed and salted storage
rows: Same password gives same stored value

example: A lab receives a test archive that a trainer protected with a short, common word. The student extracts the hash from the archive, identifies the hash type and checks it against a small wordlist in the training lab. It is found quickly. The trainer then shows that a long random passphrase resists the same method.
mistakes: Believing hashing is the same as encryption.
Thinking a hash can simply be decoded.
Forgetting to identify the hash type before choosing a method.
Testing on real accounts or files without authority.
Assuming every password can be recovered.

terms.meaning: A fixed-size value calculated from data. It is a one-way function.
A random value added to a password before hashing.
A deliberately slow method that turns a password into a key or hash.
A long password made of several words.

exam.a: So the same password gives different hashes, and precomputed results cannot be reused.

exam.q: Why does a long random password resist cracking?
exam.a: It is not in wordlists and the number of possible guesses is very large.
